title: How Universities Should Prepare Founders
gist: Paul Graham argues, drawing on 20 years of YC admissions data, that the only two things universities need to do to produce more successful startup founders are to make students believe starting a company is achievable and to give them unstructured time for their own projects — and that most institutional interventions (entrepreneurship curricula, business plan competitions, business schools) actively work against this.

themes.theme: What YC's filter reveals about founder potential

insights.claim: YC's 20-year track record of screening founders shows the dominant predictor of startup success is the ability to build things plus a demonstrated habit of doing it, not credentials like GPA or a business/entrepreneurship background.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Investors and recruiters screening early-stage founders or technical hires should weight shipped projects and building track record far more heavily than academic pedigree or an 'entrepreneurship' credential.
insights.quote: They want people who are good at building things and have a habit of doing it.
insights.locator: What do the YC partners look for?

insights.claim: The hard part of a startup is product — knowing what to build and being able to build it — and that capability comes from technical fields like computer science, mechanical engineering, or molecular biology rather than management or finance training.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Founder due diligence should probe depth of technical/product competence over pitch polish or MBA-style business planning skill.
insights.locator: The hard part of startups is product

insights.claim: Building-relevant expertise can come from unexpected, non-technical domains — Steve Jobs's study of calligraphy is cited as directly contributing to Apple's later dominance of desktop publishing — so founder-relevant skill should be defined broadly rather than restricted to STEM majors.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: When evaluating unconventional founders, an eclectic or humanities-adjacent background shouldn't be discounted if it produced deep, transferable craft skill.
insights.quote: It was useful to Steve Jobs to have studied calligraphy, for example; it was one of the reasons Apple dominated desktop publishing.
insights.locator: But building should be understood in a very broad sense

insights.claim: College major is a weak signal of founder capability: Mark Zuckerberg was a psychology major, not computer science, despite being a skilled programmer who went on to found Facebook/Meta.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Screening founders on declared major or degree field is a poor filter compared to demonstrated building ability.
insights.quote: Mark Zuckerberg was good at programming, but he was a psychology major, not a CS major.
insights.locator: And of course you don't have to major in something

insights.claim: Even in an AI-driven future where models write most code, studying computer science remains valuable because founders effectively become engineering managers who need to understand and evaluate the work being automated for them.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Bearish takes that AI coding tools make CS education obsolete are overstated for the founder/technical-leadership track; demand for people who can direct AI-generated engineering work persists.
insights.quote: And even if you have AIs writing all your code for you, you're still in the position of an engineering manager, and good engineering managers should be able to do the work of those working for them.
insights.locator: Notes [1]

themes.theme: Why side projects, not curricula, produce founders

insights.claim: YC weighs applicants' personal projects heavily and essentially ignores GPA, because projects simultaneously provide the deepest subject knowledge, the best way to find cofounders, and the best source of startup ideas.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: A founder's or candidate's history of self-initiated projects is a more actionable diligence signal than transcripts or resumes.
insights.quote: Projects are the best source of knowledge, the best source of founding teams, and the best source of startup ideas.
insights.locator: Now it should be clear why the YC partners care

insights.claim: The best startup ideas come from unstructured side projects rather than deliberate ideation, because the most promising ideas tend to look implausible at first and would be filtered out by anyone consciously searching for a startup idea.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Founders and scouts should discount formal 'idea generation' exercises and instead track what technically capable young builders are tinkering with, since that pool is disproportionately likely to seed the next big company.
insights.quote: random side projects are where the best startup ideas come from
insights.locator: Fourth, and perhaps most surprisingly

insights.claim: Because the most successful startups tend to have multiple founders, and the only reliable way to know if someone will be a good cofounder is to have already worked with them, working on side projects together functions as a de facto cofounder-vetting mechanism, as it did for Apple and Microsoft before their founding products.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Investors evaluating founding teams should check whether cofounders have a real prior collaboration history, not just a pitch-deck partnership formed for fundraising purposes.
insights.quote: Apple and Microsoft were just the last of many projects their founders had worked on together.
insights.locator: Second, working on projects together

insights.claim: Working on self-directed projects builds the specific muscle a startup requires — operating without a teacher or boss assigning tasks — making the transition to founding a company feel natural rather than disorienting.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Founder readiness assessments should look for a track record of self-directed initiative, since that predicts comfort with the ambiguity of running a company.
insights.locator: Third, a startup is a project

themes.theme: The belief gap and founder visibility

insights.claim: YC application data shows Harvard alumni apply at roughly twice the rate of Yale and Princeton alumni, a gap Graham attributes not to differences in student ability but to how customary starting a startup is at each school's culture.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: University-level startup output is partly a cultural/network effect rather than a pure talent effect, implying that schools like Yale and Princeton have latent, currently-unrealized founder supply that could be unlocked by culture-building rather than curriculum changes.
insights.quote: Harvard alumni, for example, apply at about twice the rate of Yale and Princeton alumni.
insights.locator: At the moment, the belief that it's possible

insights.claim: Merely making students believe starting a startup is a viable option could roughly double the number who attempt it at schools like Yale and Princeton, without any change to teaching content.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: A low-cost, non-curricular intervention (exposure to relatable founders) could be a high-leverage lever for universities or programs trying to increase startup formation rates.
insights.locator: Which in turn implies that merely by making

insights.claim: How inspiring a founder is to students scales roughly with their wealth and fame divided by their age gap from the audience, meaning a founder in their mid-twenties three years into a company worth a couple hundred million dollars can be more motivating as a role model than a much richer, older, famous billionaire.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Programs seeking to build a startup culture should prioritize bringing in near-peer founders with modest but real outcomes over headline billionaire speakers.
insights.quote: How inspiring founders are to students is a function roughly of how rich and famous they are divided by how much older they are than the students.
insights.locator: How inspiring founders are to students

themes.theme: Unstructured time as the hidden startup input

insights.claim: Microsoft and Meta both originated during Harvard's reading period — the gap between classes ending and final exams beginning — because it uniquely combined all students being on campus with no assignments due the next day.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Removing short-term deadline pressure for concentrated groups of talented people is a concrete, low-cost mechanism for generating high-value company formation — a template applicable beyond universities (e.g., corporate 'hack weeks' or sabbaticals).
insights.quote: Microsoft and Meta have something in common that few people realize. They both got started during reading period at Harvard.
insights.locator: Microsoft and Meta have something in common

insights.claim: Graham attributes the creation of two trillion-dollar companies (Microsoft and Meta) directly to the removal of daily coursework deadlines for a few weeks, and speculates that a permanently longer reading period at Harvard could measurably raise US GDP.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Frames unstructured time itself as an economically significant, scalable input to company formation, not just an anecdotal quirk.
insights.quote: Merely eliminating it for a few weeks resulted in two trillion dollar companies.
insights.locator: That latter constraint, especially

insights.claim: Giving all students more free time will help the most energetic and ambitious ones do much better while letting the least motivated do worse, but this is worth it because the lazy already achieve so little that there is little downside room, while the ambitious have large upside room — raising the average outcome without necessarily moving the median.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: A useful mental model for any policy (educational, corporate, or organizational) that trades average oversight for upside optionality: judge such policies by effect on the tail, not the median.
insights.quote: The price of giving the most energetic students room to do even better is that it leaves the least energetic ones room to do even worse.
insights.locator: Another reason it will be hard

insights.claim: Breakthrough student projects tend to break institutional rules — Bill Gates got in trouble for bringing non-student Paul Allen into Harvard's computer lab to work on Altair BASIC, and Mark Zuckerberg was put on disciplinary probation over Facemash — suggesting rule violation is more the norm than the exception for high-potential founder projects.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Institutions (or investors evaluating university-affiliated founders) should treat past rule-breaking or disciplinary friction around a side project as a potentially positive signal of ambition rather than a red flag.
insights.quote: Bill broke university rules by bringing Paul Allen, who wasn't a student, into the computer lab with him to work on Altair Basic. Zuck got in such trouble over Facemash that he was put on disciplinary probation.
insights.locator: And they should be left alone

insights.claim: Graham explicitly advises universities to tolerate rule-breaking student projects, citing students currently flying drones out of line of sight as an example of behavior institutions should overlook rather than police.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: A concrete, present-tense signal of where frontier student experimentation is currently happening (unregulated drone flight) that could be a lead indicator of where informal innovation is concentrated.
insights.quote: Right now there are students flying drones out of line of sight. Turn a blind eye to it.
insights.locator: Right now there are students flying drones

insights.claim: Business plan competitions are actively counterproductive because they train students to believe fundraising and pitching investors is the essential act of starting a startup, when the real task is building a product users want.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: University or accelerator programs still centered on pitch competitions are teaching a distorted model of startup success and should be redesigned or dropped in favor of building-focused formats.
insights.quote: The core of starting a startup is not creating a story that appeals to investors, but creating a product that appeals to users.
insights.locator: One common response to this inconvenient truth

insights.claim: Fundraising is a necessary but secondary task in building a startup; the essential audience to win over is users via working prototypes, not investors via narrative.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Reframes founder time allocation: investor-facing narrative work should be treated as overhead relative to product-building, informing how accelerators and early-stage investors should coach founders.
insights.quote: Fundraising is merely a necessary evil.
insights.locator: As an investor, I can tell you that's not true

insights.claim: Business schools were designed to train managers for large 20th-century industrial corporations, not founders, making them structurally mismatched to startup creation and a net negative influence when they shape a university's founder-preparation strategy.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Investors sourcing technical founders should treat an MBA/business-school credential as neutral-to-negative signal for startup-building capability versus a hard-science or engineering background.
insights.quote: they're the West Points of industrial capitalism.
insights.locator: Notes [6]

insights.claim: It is structurally impossible for universities to actually teach students how to start a startup within a degree program, because running a startup properly demands full-time commitment incompatible with coursework, and a genuine lab-style class would force students to either abandon promising companies or drop out.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Sets a hard boundary on what accelerator-style university programs can credibly promise; any program claiming to 'teach' startup creation inside a normal degree structure should be viewed skeptically.
insights.quote: Running a startup is incompatible with being a full time student. The only way to learn how to start a startup is to do it.
insights.locator: Running a startup is incompatible

insights.claim: The genuinely optimal founder-preparation strategy is nearly invisible from the outside — no new entrepreneurship curriculum, no dedicated 'Innovation Center,' no incremental spending — because it consists of teaching existing technical subjects well and giving students back unscheduled time, which risks looking to parents and prospective students like the university is doing nothing.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Explains why universities systematically over-invest in visible-but-low-value entrepreneurship theater; a university's marketing incentives are misaligned with what actually produces founders, a gap that could inform where to look for underrated founder pipelines (schools not chasing the entrepreneurship-brand trend).
insights.quote: If you have spare money, give it to the people teaching computer science or mechanical engineering or molecular biology.
insights.locator: Probably one of the reasons universities are tempted

insights.claim: Startups will never be more than about 10% of any student body, yet the recommended policy of returning free time to students would benefit essentially all ambitious and energetic students, not just would-be founders, making the change easier to justify institutionally.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Frames the reading-period/free-time intervention as a broad-based educational improvement rather than a niche startup-culture play, which matters for how such a proposal would need to be pitched to university administrators.
insights.quote: They're never going to be more than 10% of the students.
insights.locator: It may seem a bit excessive
